title: XML Sitemaps: How to Build One Google Actually Uses
excerpt: What belongs in an XML sitemap, what to leave out, how to handle lastmod and size limits, how to submit it to Google, and how to audit it against a crawl of your site.
meta_title: XML Sitemap Guide: Build, Submit and Audit
meta_description: Build an XML sitemap Google can trust: list only canonical, indexable URLs, keep lastmod honest, submit it in Search Console and audit it against a crawl.
key_takeaways: An XML sitemap should list only canonical, indexable URLs that return a 200 status.
A sitemap is a hint that helps discovery, not a guarantee that pages will be indexed.
Google uses lastmod only when it is consistently accurate and ignores priority and changefreq.
One sitemap holds up to 50,000 URLs or 50 MB uncompressed, and larger sites use a sitemap index.
Comparing your sitemap against a crawl reveals stale URLs, missing pages and orphan pages.
content_html:
Most sites have an XML sitemap these days, usually generated by a plugin nobody has looked at since launch. Open one and you may find a surprise. Picture a site with 120 real pages whose sitemap lists 900 URLs, including tag archives, redirected posts, test pages and URLs marked noindex.

That sitemap is still "working" in the sense that it exists. But it is sending Google a muddled message about which pages matter, and it hides the pages that genuinely need attention.

This guide covers what belongs in an XML sitemap, what to leave out, how to handle dates and size limits, how to submit it to Google, and how to audit it against a crawl of your site. It is one step in our technical SEO audit checklist for small sites.

What an XML sitemap is, and what it is not

An XML sitemap is a file that lists the URLs on your site you want search engines to crawl and index, optionally with the date each one last changed meaningfully.

A sitemap is a hint, not an order. It helps Google discover URLs and understand which ones you consider important, but it does not guarantee that every listed page will be crawled or indexed. Pages still have to earn their place on quality and technical grounds.

Do you even need one? Google's overview of sitemaps says you might not if your site is small (about 500 pages or fewer that you want in search), well linked internally, and has no images, videos or news content that need to show up in search. In practice, a clean sitemap costs almost nothing, so most sites should still have one.

What belongs in your XML sitemap

The rule is simple. Only list URLs that you want to appear in search, exactly as you want them to appear. Every URL in the file should be:

  • Returning a 200 status, not a redirect or an error.
  • Indexable, with no noindex in a meta robots tag or X-Robots-Tag header.
  • Canonical, meaning the page's rel="canonical" points to itself, not to another URL.
  • Crawlable, so not blocked by robots.txt.
  • Absolute and consistent, using the same protocol, host and trailing slash style as your live URLs.

Google's guide to building and submitting a sitemap asks for fully qualified, absolute URLs, so https://www.example.com/cakes/ rather than /cakes/. A minimal sitemap looks like this:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<urlset xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9">
  <url>
    <loc>https://www.example.com/wedding-cakes/</loc>
    <lastmod>2026-09-14</lastmod>
  </url>
</urlset>

What to leave out

Most sitemap problems come from listing URLs that contradict other signals on your site. Leave these out:

  • Redirected URLs. List the final destination instead. If you recently moved pages, our guide to permanent versus temporary redirects explains how to clean up after the move.
  • 404 and 410 pages. Deleted pages should drop out of the sitemap at the same time they go offline.
  • Noindexed pages. Listing a page and telling Google not to index it sends opposite signals.
  • Non-canonical duplicates, such as URLs with tracking parameters, sort orders or print versions.
  • URLs blocked by robots.txt. If you are unsure which paths your file blocks, check them against how robots.txt rules match URLs.
  • Low-value archive pages you would not want as a search result, such as empty tag pages or attachment pages.

Say you run a bakery site with a blog. Your plugin lists 40 tag archives, each with one or two posts. None of them are pages you would want a searcher to land on. Exclude them from the sitemap (and consider noindexing them) so the file points Google at your recipes and product pages instead.

Be honest with lastmod

The optional <lastmod> field tells search engines when a page last changed. It is only useful if it is true.

According to the same Google guide, Google uses lastmod when it is consistently and verifiably accurate, and it should reflect the last significant change, such as an update to the main content, structured data or links. Changing the copyright year in the footer does not count.

The same page says Google ignores <priority> and <changefreq>. You can leave them out entirely.

Do not set every lastmod to today's date on each rebuild. If every URL claims to have changed every day, the field stops carrying any information, and Google is likely to stop trusting it for your site.

Size limits and sitemap index files

A single sitemap can hold up to 50,000 URLs or 50 MB uncompressed, whichever comes first. Larger sites split their URLs across several sitemaps and list them in a sitemap index file.

Google's page on managing sitemaps with sitemap index files explains the format: a <sitemapindex> element containing one <sitemap> entry per child sitemap. You then submit only the index file.

Small sites rarely hit the limits, but splitting can still help diagnosis. Separate sitemaps for pages, posts and products let you see in Search Console which group has indexing problems, instead of one blended number.

How to submit your sitemap to Google

There are two ways to tell Google where your sitemap lives, and you can use both:

  1. Search Console. Open the Sitemaps report in Search Console, paste the sitemap URL into "Add a new sitemap" and submit. You need owner permissions on the property to do this.
  2. Robots.txt. Add a line such as Sitemap: https://www.example.com/sitemap.xml. Any crawler that reads your robots.txt can then find it.

After submitting, check that the status reads Success. If it shows "Couldn't fetch", load the sitemap URL in a private browser window. Common causes are a login requirement, a robots.txt block, or the sitemap returning an error page.

Then open the Page indexing report and filter by your submitted sitemap. That view shows how many of the URLs you asked Google to index actually made it in, and why the rest did not.

Audit your sitemap against a crawl

A sitemap tells you what you think your site contains. A crawl tells you what is actually reachable. The useful findings live in the gap between the two.

Crawl your site with sitemap seeding turned on, so the crawler starts from both your home page and the sitemap URLs. A free desktop crawler like Scary Spider SEO flags all three mismatches below automatically.

FindingWhat it usually meansFix
Non-200 or non-indexable URLs in the sitemapThe sitemap is stale or the generator ignores redirects and noindexRemove them, or fix the generator setting
Indexable pages missing from the sitemapCustom pages or post types the generator skipsInclude that content type, or add the URLs
Orphan pages: in the sitemap but not linked internallyOld landing pages, or pages dropped from the menuLink to them from relevant pages, or retire them

Orphan pages deserve a second look. If a page matters enough to be in your sitemap, it matters enough to be linked from somewhere on your site. If it does not, ask whether it should exist at all.

Common sitemap problems in popular CMS setups

Most sitemaps are generated automatically, so problems tend to come from settings rather than typos. Watch for:

  • Two sitemaps from two plugins, for example the CMS's built-in one and an SEO plugin's, both submitted with overlapping URLs. Pick one and remove the other.
  • Every content type included by default, including tags, authors, media attachments or custom types that have no search value.
  • Staging or development URLs leaking in after a migration because the site address setting was not updated.
  • A cached sitemap that a caching plugin or CDN serves long after pages change.

The fix is usually one settings change, then a fresh crawl to confirm the sitemap matches reality.

The bottom line

A good XML sitemap is a short, honest list: canonical, indexable URLs that return 200, with lastmod dates that only change when the content does. Everything else adds noise.

Submit it in Search Console and robots.txt, then audit it against a crawl regularly. The gaps between your sitemap and your real site structure point straight at the pages that need fixing.

Your next step: open your sitemap in a browser, pick ten URLs at random, and check that each one loads, is indexable and points its canonical at itself.

faqs.question: Where do I find my website's sitemap?
faqs.answer: Try yoursite.com/sitemap.xml or yoursite.com/sitemap_index.xml, and check the Sitemap line in yoursite.com/robots.txt. Your CMS or SEO plugin settings will also show the sitemap URL it generates.

faqs.question: How often should I update my XML sitemap?
faqs.answer: Whenever pages are added, removed or meaningfully changed. Most CMS sitemaps update automatically, so the real task is checking that the generator settings exclude redirects, noindexed pages and low-value archives.

faqs.question: Do I need to resubmit my sitemap after every change?
faqs.answer: No. Once Google knows where your sitemap is, it fetches it again on its own. Resubmitting is useful after a major change, such as a site migration or a new sitemap URL.

faqs.question: Should images be in my XML sitemap?
faqs.answer: You can add image entries using Google's image sitemap extension, which can help Google find images it might otherwise miss. For most small sites with images in normal img tags, it is optional.
